title: Work with excellence
hook: a hadith: God loves that when you do a work, you do it with excellence (al-Bayhaqi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hadith about bread you earn yourself. Your line was bread you paid for. What did you eat that came from your own work? Today, the same tradition asks how the work is done. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

The underside of a drawer. Nobody will ever see it. The customer opens the drawer, takes out a spoon, and never once turns it over. And still some carpenters sand that hidden side smooth, the same as the front. Ask why, and the answer may have nothing to do with money. Muslims have a narration that speaks to exactly this. It's recorded in the hadith collection of al-Bayhaqi, and it says, in paraphrase, that when one of you does a piece of work, God loves that it be done with excellence. Not the work people watch. Any work. Today's word is the name for that kind of care.
screen: `THE UNDERSIDE OF A DRAWER.` → `NOBODY SEES IT.` → `GOD LOVES WORK DONE WELL.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ihsan is an Arabic word put into English as excellence, or doing what is beautiful. It comes up in a scene recorded in Sahih Muslim. A stranger in very white clothes sits down knee to knee with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asks him questions. What is islam? What is iman, faith? And then, what is ihsan? The answer, in paraphrase: to worship God as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, to know that He sees you. After the stranger leaves, the Prophet tells his companions that it was the angel Gabriel, come to teach them their religion. So in this teaching, ihsan begins as a way of standing before God. Second, it doesn't stay in the prayer hall. Another hadith in Sahih Muslim says God has prescribed ihsan in all things. And the example it gives is not a mosque or a sermon. It's a knife. When you slaughter an animal, sharpen your blade and spare the animal. Excellence reaches all the way down to the edge of a butcher's knife. Third, the narration from al-Bayhaqi takes it into the workshop: God loves that when you do a work, you do it well. Put the three side by side and a picture forms. Muslim teachers describe ihsan as doing a thing as though it's seen, because, in their faith, it is. In that telling, the underside of the drawer is not hidden from God. Fourth, what this asks of an ordinary afternoon. It isn't perfectionism, the anxious kind that never finishes. It's attention. The email read once more before sending. The bandage put on gently. The rice washed properly. Excellence, in this telling, is less about being the best and more about not cutting the corner nobody would notice.
screen: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.` · `IHSAN IN ALL THINGS.` · `GOD LOVES WORK DONE WELL.` · `ATTENTION, NOT PERFECTIONISM.` · then, large: `IHSAN.`

segments.voice: Make the sitting itself the piece of work. Set your feet with care. Let the back lengthen, not stiff, just upright. Place your hands where they can rest, the way a carpenter sets down a finished drawer. Now give the next breath your full attention: the start of it, the turn at the top, the long way out. Then the next one. When the mind wanders off, come back without fuss, the way you would sand one more stroke on a side nobody sees. If you pray, you can sit as though seen, in your own tradition's way. If you don't, simply let the breath have your care. The bell holds the time.
Ihsan. An Arabic word for excellence, doing what is beautiful, as though seen by God. Today's word.
Your line: excellence. Today, do one task excellently, including the part nobody will check. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of ihsan both in worship, praying as though seeing God, and in daily work, and teachers often cite the hadith that God loves work done with excellence when talking about jobs, crafts and study.

fork.setup: you're sanding a drawer. the underside will never be seen by anyone. what does the narration about excellence point toward?

sand it only if the customer asks.
fork.reveal: the narration says God loves work done with excellence, any work, not only the work people watch.

original.note: Arabic: excellence, doing what is beautiful; in the hadith of Gabriel, worshiping as though you see God.

trapdoor: what you thought: being the best at something.
what it means: doing a thing well and with care, as though it's seen, because in Muslim faith God sees it.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of Gabriel in Sahih Muslim, where ihsan is asked about after islam and iman, and a second hadith there: God has prescribed ihsan in all things.

sources.ref: al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman (God loves that when one of you does a work, he does it well)

notes: The al-Bayhaqi narration's Arabic verb is generally given as yutqinahu (from itqan, precision/excellence), not ihsan. The index word is ihsan, so the script ties the narration to ihsan through Sahih Muslim 8 and 1955 rather than claiming the narration uses the word ihsan. A Muslim Keeper should confirm this framing and the narration's grading.
Confirm hadith numbering: Sahih Muslim 8 (Gabriel: islam, iman, ihsan) and Sahih Muslim 1955 (God has prescribed ihsan in all things; sharpen the blade).
'A stranger in very white clothes ... knee to knee' paraphrases details of Sahih Muslim 8; confirm.
'Muslim teachers describe ihsan as doing a thing as though it's seen' is an attribution, not a count; confirm phrasing.
All hadith paraphrased; no English hadith translation quoted.
